# Tobit Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_001_page_001.jpg

---

**1** This is the story of Tobit — a man whose family tree stretched back through Tobiel, Ananiel, Aduel, Gabael, Raphael, and Raguel to the ancient clan of Asiel, of the tribe of Naphtali.

**2** He had been taken prisoner by the Assyrian king Enemessar, torn from his hometown of Thisbe — a village on the southern edge of Kedesh-Naphtali, in the upper hills of Galilee, west of Asher, near the ridge above Phogor.

**3** Let me tell you about myself. My name is Tobit, and all my life I tried to walk a straight path — doing what was right, showing kindness wherever I could. Even after we were dragged off to Nineveh, deep in Assyrian territory, I kept faith with my people and looked after whoever I could.

**4** When I was still a boy back in Israel, the whole tribe of Naphtali — my own people — walked away from Jerusalem. That city had been chosen above all others as the place where God would be worshipped, where the great temple had been built to stand forever. But they turned their backs on it.

**5** Instead, they joined the other rebel tribes and the dynasty of Jeroboam in bowing down to the golden calf of Baal.

**6** I refused. Every year, while everyone around me was offering sacrifices to false gods, I made the journey to Jerusalem alone to keep the appointed festivals — as the law requires. I brought my firstfruits and tithes of grain, the firstborn of my flocks, the first wool of the shearing season.

**7** I handed the grain, wine, oil, pomegranates, figs, and all the rest directly to the priests — the sons of Aaron — at the altar. The Levites who served in Jerusalem got their portion too. For six years running I converted the second tithe into silver, traveled to Jerusalem, and spent it there each year as prescribed.

**8** Every third year I set the third tithe aside for widows, orphans, and the foreigners who had thrown in their lot with Israel. We ate it together according to what Moses commanded and what my grandmother Deborah — Ananiel's mother — had taught us. I was an orphan myself; my father had died young.

**9** When I was old enough, I married a woman from our own family named Anna. She gave me a son, and we called him Tobias.

**10** Then the Assyrians came for us. I was taken prisoner and brought to Nineveh. Once there, all my relatives and neighbors gave in and started eating Gentile food —

**11** but not me. I held the line.

**12** God was always in my heart, and I was not going to forget it now.

**13** God rewarded that faithfulness. He gave me a place of favor and respect in Enemessar's eyes, and I became the king's personal purchasing agent.

**14** I traveled regularly to Media, buying goods for the king. Before he died, I managed to deposit ten talents of silver with a trustworthy man named Gabael — brother of Gabrias — over in Media, for safekeeping.

**15** But when Enemessar died and his son Sennacherib took the throne, the roads to Media became too dangerous to travel. My trips there were finished.

**16** All through the reign of Enemessar, I had been doing what I could for my people —

**17** sharing my food with the hungry, giving clothes to the naked. And whenever I found the body of one of my people thrown outside the walls of Nineveh like garbage, I buried them.

**18** Sennacherib was brutal. He came back from his defeat in Judea — the catastrophe that God brought on him for his arrogance and blasphemy — in a murderous rage, killing Israelites right and left. I went out at night to recover the bodies and bury them in secret. He sent soldiers looking for them and found nothing.

**19** But someone told on me. A Ninevite went to the king and informed him I was the one burying the bodies. When I found out I had been denounced and that Sennacherib wanted me dead, I ran.

**20** They seized everything I had. My house, my land, my savings — gone. All I had left was Anna and Tobias.

**21** It didn't last long. Within forty days, two of Sennacherib's own sons stabbed him in his sleep and fled to the mountains of Ararat. His son Esarhaddon took the throne. He put my nephew Achiacharus — son of my brother Anael — in charge of all the royal accounts and the entire administration.

**22** Achiacharus spoke up for me, and I was allowed to come home to Nineveh. My nephew was a man of enormous power — chief cupbearer, keeper of the royal seal, steward, treasurer, second only to the king. And he was family.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

- Verse 3: PNEUMA opens with "Let me tell you about myself" to honor the first-person autobiographical register of Tobit's voice. The book is deliberately self-presentation; Tobit is giving testimony.
- Verse 5: "bowing down to the golden calf of Baal" — the Greek mentions "the heifer Baal"; PNEUMA clarifies the idolatrous act while preserving its contemptuous framing.
- Verse 8: "grandmother Deborah" — the GII text uniquely names her; PNEUMA highlights her role as a moral teacher since it anchors Tobit's piety in family transmission.
- Verse 11: "I held the line" — PNEUMA renders the Greek's studied understatement with an equally terse English phrase to match the rhetorical effect.
- Verse 18: The emotional texture of the burial scene is crucial; Sennacherib's murderous return after the Judean defeat (cf. 2 Kgs 19; Isa 37) connects Tobit to larger Israelite history.
- Verse 21: "stabbed him in his sleep" is implied by "killed him" plus the historical record; PNEUMA makes the scene vivid without over-specifying.
- "Sarchedonus" rendered as "Esarhaddon" for modern readers' recognition.

*— PNEUMA*
